Have you heard of Eadweard Muybridge? You might be interested in his work. He produced it back in the 19th century but it's still used to teach animation today.

Sure enough its gait pattern has two paws (either both left or both right side) in the air simultaneously. So the dog is more like a person in the sense of constantly "falling" onto it's feet with each step, whereas the cat has at least one limb planted on both sides throughout.

The cat also (briefly) has only two limbs supporting it during the "plant" position when one of the rear legs replaces one of the forelegs.

Regardless how many paws it has on the ground at any one time though, all of those paws are in a straight line, otherwise it would end up with two sets of tracks.

This is in contrast to most quadropeds who walk with their legs more spread so that the three legs they have on the ground form a triangle.

EDIT: Had to look up a couple videos of dogs and big cats sprinting in slow motion. Sprinting changes everything. They launch off both hind feet and only momentarily touch with the front legs just to maintain their uprightness until the next "jump". So sprinting for four-leggers is basically like really fast forward jumping.
